⚠️ Closed alpha — provisional docs. OpenDefence on Kubernetes (opendefence-platform) is in closed alpha and under rapid, breaking development. This page describes a moving target and will most likely be superseded by the documentation that ships with the first public release — treat everything here as provisional, and do not rely on it for a production deployment.

This page maps the network edge of the platform: the Traefik instance that terminates HTTPS for every web-facing hostname, and the raw TCP/UDP ports that deliberately bypass it. Read it when you need to know exactly what listens where, which hostname reaches which backend, and how exposure differs between the local kind cluster and a cloud k3s deployment.

The edge at a glance

Everything that listens at the cluster boundary falls into three groups: the two Traefik entrypoints (:80 and :443), Keycloak's own TLS listener on :9443, and three raw TCP/UDP Services for protocol-native clients. The following diagram shows all of them and where their traffic ends up.

blocks.html:
Traefik deployment

Traefik is installed in **infra-phase1** into the traefik-system namespace, rendered by Kustomize from two Helm charts declared in k8s/traefik/base/kustomization.yaml:

  • **traefik-crds** 1.13.0 with gatewayAPI: true in values-crds.yaml, so the Gateway API CRDs are installed alongside the Traefik ones. Routing today is done entirely with IngressRoute resources; the Gateway API surface is available but not yet what the app manifests use.
  • **traefik** 38.0.1 with values-traefik-plugins.yaml.

The values file sets the pieces the rest of the platform depends on:

  • --providers.kubernetescrd.allowCrossNamespace=true. This is load-bearing: IngressRoutes live in each app's namespace but reference Middlewares in traefik-system and TLSOptions in opendefence-system. Without cross-namespace references none of the routes below would resolve.
  • Entrypoints: web on :80 exists only to issue a permanent redirect to websecure on :443 (and, on cloud, to answer Let's Encrypt HTTP-01 challenges — see below). All application traffic rides websecure.
  • A default middleware on **websecure**: traefik-system-strip-identity-headers@kubernetescrd. The strip-identity-headers Middleware (k8s/traefik/middleware/base/strip-identity-headers-middleware.yaml) unconditionally clears every client-suppliable identity header before anything else runs: X-ClientCert-DN, X-ClientCert-Serial, X-SSL-Client-Verify, X-SSL-Client-Fingerprint, Callsign, Callsign-Valid, Callsign-Valid-Reason, l5d-client-id, X-Forwarded-Tls-Client-Cert, X-Forwarded-Tls-Client-Cert-Info, Validity-Secret. Backends trust these headers precisely because Traefik guarantees a client can never smuggle its own values in — any of them present downstream was set by the edge, not the caller.
  • Three in-repo Go plugins (callsign-validity, callsign-redirect, legacy-mtls-headers) mounted from ConfigMaps as Traefik experimental **localPlugins** (Yaegi-interpreted), plus the RM_CALLSIGN_VALIDITY_SECRET env var they need, fed from a Secret mirrored into traefik-system. What the plugins actually do is covered in Edge mTLS & callsign checks.

The Deployment is patched to strategy: Recreate (the rolling-update block is removed). Locally Traefik binds host ports, so two pods cannot coexist; the trade-off is that every Traefik redeploy briefly drops the whole HTTPS edge.

Hostname map

All hostnames resolve to the cluster's external IP and are served by Traefik on 443, except kc.<domain> which is Keycloak's own TLS on 9443. <domain> is the per-deployment host: the Zarf variable OPENDEFENCE_HOST (templated as ###ZARF_VAR_OPENDEFENCE_HOST### in cloud manifests), and always localmaeher.dev.pvarki.fi on a local kind cluster. The authoritative source is docs/endpoints.md in the platform repo.

Host Backend Edge mTLS

mtls.<domain> rmui + rmapi /api behind client certs; product UIs at /ui/tak, /ui/mtx, /ui/matrix; /ca redirects back to the base domain mtls-optional
bl.<domain> Battlelog (battlelog:80) mtls-strict
mtx.<domain> MediaMTX integration API /api (mtx-server-internal:8005) mtls-strict
tak.<domain> TAK integration API /api and /ephemeral/api (tak-server:8003) mtls-optional
matrix.<domain> Matrix integration API /api (matrix:8012) mtls-strict
synapse.<domain> Synapse (synapse-server:8008); /_synapse/admin allow-listed to 127.0.0.1/32; login/logout/refresh paths rerouted to MAS (mas:8080) none
mas.<domain> Matrix Authentication Service (mas:8080) none

The mTLS column names the Traefik TLSOption attached to the route: mtls-optional (VerifyClientCertIfGiven) lets browsers in without a certificate, mtls-strict (RequireAndVerifyClientCert) refuses the TLS handshake without a valid client cert. Both verify against the internal CA bundle — semantics and the callsign plugins are on Edge mTLS & callsign checks.

IngressRoutes

Each app ships its IngressRoutes in its overlays, not its base — the local and cloud variants differ only in the hostname literal (hard-coded localmaeher.dev.pvarki.fi vs the ###ZARF_VAR_OPENDEFENCE_HOST### template) and in which issuer signs the server certificate. Routes match on Host(`…`) plus PathPrefix, with explicit priority values where several rules share a host. A representative route, the MediaMTX integration API:

## k8s/app-mtx/overlays/local/mtx.ingressroute.yaml (first document)
apiVersion: traefik.io/v1alpha1
kind: IngressRoute
metadata:
  name: mtx
  namespace: app-mtx
spec:
  entryPoints:
  - websecure
  routes:
  - match: Host(`mtx.localmaeher.dev.pvarki.fi`) && PathPrefix(`/api`)
    kind: Rule
    priority: 110
    middlewares:
    - name: mtls-chain-with-legacy
      namespace: traefik-system
    services:
    - name: mtx-server-internal
      port: mtxrmapi
  tls:
    secretName: mtx-tls
    options:
      name: mtls-strict
      namespace: opendefence-system

Every route follows the same anatomy:

  • **tls.secretName** — a per-host server certificate minted by cert-manager. Locally these come from the internal CA (intermediate-ca-issuer / ca-issuer); on cloud, browser-facing hosts use Let's Encrypt instead (see below). Details on the chain are in PKI & trust.
  • **tls.options** — a cross-namespace reference to TLSOption mtls-optional or mtls-strict in opendefence-system (k8s/opendefence-system/overlays/<env>/mtls.tlsoption.yaml), which controls client-certificate verification for that host.
  • **middlewares** — mTLS-protected routes attach mtls-chain (or mtls-chain-with-legacy for backends that still read X-ClientCert-* headers) from traefik-system. The chains wrap the callsign-validity plugins; their internals belong to Edge mTLS & callsign checks.

A few routes are special-cased: matrix-wellknown serves /.well-known/matrix on the root domain from the matrix pod's nginx; synapse-server carries an ipAllowList middleware (synapse-admin-deny, 127.0.0.1/32) in front of /_synapse/admin and reroutes MAS-compatibility login paths to mas:8080; matrix-rtc strips the /livekit/jwt and /livekit/sfu prefixes; and rmui-mtls permanently redirects /ca* from the mTLS host back to the base domain (the mtls-ca-redirect redirectRegex middleware), so certificate downloads never require a client cert.

Inside Traefik every HTTPS request on websecure passes through the same pipeline before it reaches a backend Service:

blocks.html:
What bypasses Traefik

Four listeners deliberately skip the HTTPS front door. The reason is protocol, not oversight: CoT streaming, RTMPS/RTSPS/SRT, and WebRTC/TURN are TCP/UDP protocols with their own framing and their own TLS — they cannot ride an HTTP reverse proxy. Keycloak could technically sit behind Traefik, but it performs its own certificate-based client authentication, so it keeps its own TLS listener.

Keycloak — **hostPort** 9443. The keycloak Deployment (opendefence-system) binds hostPort: 9443 directly on the node in both environments; the ghcr.io/pvarki/keycloak-server image is pre-built with its own TLS listener and --https-client-auth=request, trusting the platform CA bundle. It is also a Linkerd opaque port, so the mesh passes the TLS bytes through untouched.

**tak-server-external** (app-tak) — TAK protocol ports, per docs/endpoints.md:

Port Proto Usage
8089 TCP CoT streaming / config
8443 TCP secure (client cert)
9000 TCP federation v1
9001 TCP federation v2
9002 TCP federation auth
8090–8094 TCP data feeds 1–5

**mtx-server** (app-mtx) — MediaMTX ingest and playback:

Port Proto Usage
1936 TCP RTMPS
8322 TCP RTSPS
8890 TCP + UDP SRT
9888 TCP HLS
9889 TCP WebRTC
9996 TCP playback
9997 TCP control API

A second Service, mtx-server-debug (9998 metrics, 9999 pprof), exists only in the local overlay and is bound to 127.0.0.1 by the kind port mappings.

**matrix-rtc-media** (app-matrix) — LiveKit / Element Call media:

Port Proto Usage
7881 TCP ICE/TCP
7882 UDP media / RTP
3478 UDP TURN
5349 TCP TURN/TLS

What each port means to its product (which clients connect where, in what order) belongs to the product books — see TAK stack (Kubernetes), MediaMTX stack (Kubernetes) and Matrix stack (Kubernetes).

The listeners are identical in both environments; only the mechanism that gets packets to them differs.

blocks.html:
Local (kind). The local Traefik overlay (k8s/traefik/overlays/local/patch-traefik.yaml) puts the Traefik pod on hostNetwork: true with hostPort 80/443 and dnsPolicy: ClusterFirstWithHostNet. The raw services become type: NodePort with nodePort set to the real port number — possible because kind-config.yaml widens the API server's service-node-port-range to 1024-9999. kind-config.yaml then maps every one of those node ports to the developer machine via extraPortMappings: 80/443/9443 and all TAK ports listen on 127.0.0.1 only, while the MediaMTX ingest/streaming ports (1936, 8322, 8890 TCP+UDP, 9888, 9889) and all LiveKit ports listen on 0.0.0.0; the MediaMTX playback, control-API and debug ports (9996–9999) stay on 127.0.0.1. A CoreDNS patch applied first in the local deploy makes in-cluster pods resolve *.localmaeher.dev.pvarki.fi to the kind node's InternalIP, so pods reach the exposed hostnames through the same entrypoints external clients use — see Deployment model.

Cloud (k3s). Traefik keeps the chart's default exposure (a LoadBalancer Service on 80/443). The raw services switch to type: LoadBalancer with allocateLoadBalancerNodePorts: false — the k3s ServiceLB (or an external LB) delivers traffic directly, so allocating throwaway 30000-range node ports would be pointless. matrix-rtc-media additionally sets externalTrafficPolicy: Local to preserve the real client source IP, which TURN and LiveKit need. Public server certificates for browser-facing hosts come from the letsencrypt-http01-staging / letsencrypt-http01-production ClusterIssuers (added only in the cloud infra-phase2; HTTP-01 solver via ingressClassName: traefik) — which is the second reason port 80 stays open on cloud: it answers ACME challenges. The internal CA still signs everything on the mTLS and mesh side.

One honest caveat for both environments: the edge is a single Traefik replica with strategy: Recreate and the in-repo plugins rely on Traefik's experimental local-plugin support — acceptable for a closed alpha, not yet a hardened production edge.
